newsitem.title: UK: Russian platinum stocks to last at least 12 months.
newsitem.headline: Russian platinum stocks to last at least 12 months.

text.p: Russian exports of platinum from government stockpiles could continue for at least 12 to 18 months if Russia is to maintain its current world supply level, a senior Johannesburg-based mining research analyst said on Thursday.

Rene Hochreiter a senior analyst with Standard Equities, a division of Standard Bank, estimated Russia had about 650,000 ounces of platinum in its stockpile, although he admitted this figure was not "robust".
Russia supplied about 23 percent of world platinum needs last year compared with an average of about 19 percent over the past ten years, he said.
Hochreiter was in London to attend the launch of Standard Bank's Platinum yearbook 1997.
He also noted that even if Russia reduced its exports to no more than its annual refined platinum production, the South African producers could increase output to fill the gap "within a year or two".
"The South African producers could add 500,000 ounces to output quite easily but they do not because they do not want to damage the price," he told Reuters.
Last year Russia exported about 1.10 million ounces of platinum of which 580,000 was newly mined from the country's Norilsk mining and refining complex.

Hochreiter estimated this year's exports at 850,000 ounces of which production would account for 560,000 ounces with 290,000 coming from stock. He said he calculated the figure on the basis of Russia's Norilsk orebody platinum-palladium of 1:4 ratio and taking a palladium stockpile estimated at 20 million ounces at "the time of Glasnost", the platinum stocks had been worked down to the current estimated figure since.
"But that doesn't account for secondary production of domestically produced platinum scrap," he said.
He described Norilsk as "a dinosaur" at which the only power supply -- its natural gas field -- was running out and could only be replaced at a cost of $60 million.
But production went up every year. "The Russians are very intelligent people who have a knack of keeping things going," he said.
Standard Bank's Platinum yearbook forecast platinum prices in a range of $330-$400 this year which compared with an average London platinum fixing of $397.175 last year and $424.22 in 1995.
Given that platinum consumption was unlikely to be more than steady this year and focused on Japanese jewellery demand, price influences could come from outside the market.
"Political moves are likely to impact platinum in 1997," said the books author Trevor Pitts.
"Russia has done so already and South African politics could have an impression later in the year," he said.
The year book estimated palladium in a $100-$150 price range this year. Last year's average fixing was $128.118, down 15 percent from 1995's $151.28
